How to read results: each row is one entry from the test set. The counter shows how many requests completed successfully out of the total. The result applies only to this run, current network, and selected domains; it does not guarantee other sites will work. The Apply button copies the selected entry into the current command configuration.

Pause before checking a site and between tested entries. In the current implementation, one field unit equals 0.5 seconds. A longer pause makes the run take longer but does not make a network configuration better.
How many times the tester repeats a request to each domain. More repeats mean more requests and a longer test; they do not guarantee a more accurate result.
How many requests the tester may run at once. This affects simultaneous network and device load; excessive load can cause delays and errors.
How long the tester waits for one request. Too little time may mark a slow site as unavailable; more time makes the test longer.

The current values and the purpose of each field are shown below. These options affect traffic handling. There is no universally correct combination for every network. Changes may affect compatibility or connectivity. Leave a field unchanged when you are unsure what it does.

This section configures the test process: pauses, request counts, and the list of checked addresses. It does not tell you which DPI value is best. Longer or more parallel tests change load and duration; results do not guarantee performance in every network.

This is a text command line, not a regular settings form. Each argument can change engine behavior. Do not edit arguments manually when you do not understand them; use the standard editor explanations and save a backup first.
The language used for labels and messages. It does not affect the network connection.
Changes only the app appearance: light, dark, or system theme.
VPN uses the Android system VPN interface for selected traffic. Proxy opens a local proxy port. These are different traffic paths; stop the service before switching.
DNS translates a site name into a network address. It affects address lookup but does not guarantee that a site is reachable. System Private DNS takes precedence when configured.
Allows IPv6 in VPN mode. It only applies when the current network has an IPv6 address and route. This switch cannot create IPv6 support where none exists.
Controls which apps are covered by the VPN. None disables list filtering; blacklist excludes selected apps; whitelist includes only selected apps.
The list of apps affected by the filter above. Changing this list changes which apps use the VPN.
Allows the app service to start after the phone boots. It does not mean the connection starts automatically.
Starts the service automatically when the app is opened. It does not change network parameters or choose settings for you.
Selects where ByeDPI settings come from: the standard field editor or the text command line. Only one editor is active at a time.
Opens the standard editor with separate fields and switches. Its values are saved in app settings.
Opens the command-line editor. This is a text format for experienced users; changing arguments at random may prevent startup.
Opens the test screen for the saved command set. Results describe only that run and the selected list of sites.
The local address where the app accepts proxy connections. This is not a website address or the external IP assigned to your phone. An invalid address can make the proxy unavailable.
The local proxy port — the connection point on the phone. If another service already uses it, the proxy may fail to start.
Excluding the app from battery optimization helps Android avoid stopping its background service. It may increase battery use.
This permission is used for some import, export, and file operations. It does not change network settings.
Maximum simultaneous connections served by the local engine. A larger number does not mean faster internet; it may use more memory and resources.
Temporary storage size for network data. It changes memory usage during transfer; very large values may waste memory.
Disables domain-related handling in the engine. This changes how it works with site names; features that rely on domains may behave differently.
Enables TCP Fast Open support when available on the system and the other endpoint. If support is unavailable, it may have no effect; compatibility depends on the network.
Defines which domains the list rule applies to: all, exclusions in a blacklist, or only entries in a whitelist. An empty or incorrect list can produce unexpected coverage.
Domains excluded from the selected handling when blacklist mode is active. Each entry is a site name; editing the list changes the rule coverage.
Domains covered by the selected handling when whitelist mode is active. Editing the list changes which sites the rule applies to.

TTL is the lifetime counter of an IP packet: network nodes decrease it, and the packet stops being forwarded when it reaches zero. This field changes the default TTL used by the engine. An unsuitable value can disrupt delivery.

Selects an internal traffic-processing method. Different options change the structure or order of data transmission. The name alone cannot tell which option is compatible with a particular network; there is no universal recommendation.
Specifies where the data stream is divided. Changing it moves the boundary between parts of a request; an unsuitable position can change how the other endpoint parses it.
Changes the split boundary so that it is tied to the part of the request containing the Host name.
Changes handling of TCP SACK, a mechanism that reports received data blocks. Disabling this information may affect TCP transfer efficiency and reliability.
TTL of the additional artificial packet. It is not the TTL of the phone or of all regular packets; an unsuitable value may cause that packet to be lost.
The offset sets the position of data inside an additional artificial packet. It changes the contents of that packet; an unsuitable value may make it invalid.
SNI is the server name sent at the start of a TLS connection. Here it is used in an additional artificial packet; changing it changes the name carried there, not the system DNS on your phone.
A single control character used by the out-of-band TCP mode. Changing it changes the contents of that control field; an arbitrary character may be unsuitable.
Allows the selected processing to be applied to HTTP traffic. When off, that processing is not applied to HTTP.
Allows the selected processing to be applied to HTTPS/TLS traffic. When off, that processing is not applied to HTTPS.
Allows the selected processing to be applied to UDP traffic. UDP is separate from TCP; this switch does not affect ordinary TCP connections.
Changes the letter case in the Host field of an HTTP request. The site address remains the same in meaning, but the header format changes.
Changes the letter case of the domain name inside an HTTP request. Some unusual servers or intermediate systems may handle that format differently.
Removes spaces from the Host field of an HTTP request. This changes the header format; an unusual original value may become invalid.
Enables splitting a TLS record into parts. This changes the structure of TLS data transmission; it does not decrypt traffic or change a certificate.
The position where a TLS record is split. It changes the boundary in the protected handshake; one DNS test cannot determine a correct value.
Ties the TLS record split position to the SNI area — the server name at the start of a TLS handshake. It changes the split location, not the site name.
The number of additional artificial UDP packets used by the selected mode. It changes extra traffic volume and load; there is no universal suitable value.
The server name inserted into the SNI field for test commands containing the corresponding placeholder. It changes the test TLS request, not the system DNS.
When enabled, the tester uses your command list instead of the built-in list. This changes which configurations are tested; unknown commands may cause test errors.
Text list of test commands: each non-empty line is treated as a separate entry. This content determines what will run; do not paste unknown lines.
The list of domains opened by the tester. Changing it changes which addresses are checked; results apply only to this list and this run.
Each result row refers to one tested entry. The counter shows how many requests succeeded out of the total. This is one test run, not a guarantee for every site or network.

This stores the text configuration used by the engine. Changing arguments changes startup parameters; the app cannot turn an unknown combination into a reliable recommendation. Save a copy before editing.
History stores previously used text configurations. Tapping an entry opens actions: apply, pin, rename, edit, copy, or delete. Applying an entry changes the active configuration.
Does not use an additional stream-processing method.
Divides the data stream into separate parts. This changes data transmission boundaries.
Changes the order in which stream parts are sent. This affects the order in which data is received.
Adds an additional artificially formed packet to the transfer. Its contents depend on other editor fields.
Uses a separate TCP out-of-band data mechanism. This is a special part of TCP exchange.
Combines TCP out-of-band data with a change in transmission order.
The domain list rule is not applied.
Domains in the blacklist are excluded from the selected handling; other domains are not listed.
The selected handling applies only to domains in the whitelist.
